posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain with a specific observation about explainability being the real blocker, not AI itself
posts.draft_comment: The ban isn't really about ChatGPT — it's about audit trails. A number without a lineage is just a guess with a confident font. We kept seeing this: teams loved the output, then froze the moment someone upstream asked 'show your working'. What does your analytics stack look like when it has to defend itself in a room with a regulator?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the trust gap insight, add the 'data provenance' layer nobody builds for
posts.draft_comment: The trust problem is almost always the same thing underneath — nobody knows where the number came from. Not really. So when it's board time, nobody wants to be the person who quoted a dashboard that turned out to pull from last month's sync. Excel feels safer because at least you can trace your steps. Have you found anything that actually closes that gap, or does it just slowly rebuild itself?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add depth on why most teams never make that cut, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a way of saying 'we don't know what matters yet.' The hard part isn't cutting the dashboard — it's getting the room to agree on which 5 actually connect to decisions people are making that week. Most teams never have that conversation, so the dashboard just grows instead. What finally forced the call for you?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing and add the insight that the problem isn't access to data, it's the absence of agreed meaning before the tool is ever opened
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone gets access, nobody gets alignment first — and then the tool gets blamed for a people-and-process problem that existed long before the licenses were bought. Democratising data only works if you've democratised the definitions underneath it. Curious whether anyone's actually solved that without just creating a new centralised bottleneck.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe from accuracy to trust/risk, add the specific layer about audit trails being the missing piece
posts.draft_comment: The framing shift here is important — accuracy issues get filed as tech debt, risk issues get escalated to the board. The problem I keep seeing is that most AI analytics tools can't show their working. No lineage, no confidence signal, no way to trace where a number came from. How are security teams supposed to audit something that can't explain itself?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: COO at a similarly-sized firm is engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the real cost of shelfware, add the insight that ease-of-build isn't the same as ease-of-use
posts.draft_comment: The £200k is almost the smaller problem. The real cost is 12 months of decisions made on gut feel because no one else could get an answer out of the thing. Most BI tools are basically built to impress in a demo — they're optimised for the moment of sale, not the moment a ops manager needs a quick answer on a Monday morning. How many times does the industry have to watch this happen before 'self-service' means something real?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market manufacturer has surfaced the classic data trust problem — validate that culture is part of it, but add the missing layer: the tooling itself creates the conditions for filter chaos
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets, one dataset — that's not a culture problem, that's a system that never made the 'right' version obvious enough. Culture gets blamed a lot for things that tooling quietly enables. The CFO doesn't care who applied which filter. They just stopped trusting the dashboard — and that's really hard to earn back.

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with enterprise AI — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem and reframe it as a data literacy gap, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: That 12% number is pretty telling — and I'd bet the 88% aren't lazy, they just don't have a clear mental model of what the tool is actually good at. Shadow AI on personal phones is the symptom, but the root is that most people don't think in queries, they think in questions they're embarrassed to ask out loud. Locking down the tool solves the compliance problem but completely ignores that one. Curious whether the 12% who stuck with it had any common thread — role, team, anything?
